exact_text: A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.
provision_summary: Providers must run a documented, continuous and iterative risk management process across the whole lifecycle of a high-risk AI system. It covers identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating risks from post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures so that residual risk is judged acceptable. Systems must be tested, including before being placed on the market, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds (Art. 9(6)-(8)). Providers must consider likely adverse impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).
responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).

exact_text: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
provision_summary: High-risk AI systems trained on data must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet quality criteria. Data governance practices must cover design choices, data origin and collection, preparation steps such as labelling and cleaning, assumptions, the suitability of the data, examination for possible biases with measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them, and the identification of data gaps. Data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, as error-free and complete as possible, and suited to the setting in which the system is intended to be used.

exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately.
provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their outputs and use them appropriately. They must come with instructions for use giving concise, complete, correct and clear information. At minimum this includes the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, its capabilities and limitations, its accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risk circumstances, any capabilities for explaining outputs, human oversight measures, maintenance needs and log-handling mechanisms.
responsible_party: AI provider (information duty owed to deployers)
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must use systems in accordance with the instructions for use (Art. 26(1); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37), with deployer breaches finable under Art. 99(4)(e).

exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Oversight measures must be proportionate to risk, autonomy and context, and may be built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. The system must be provided to the deployer so that the people assigned to oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to understand its capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret its outputs, decide not to use or to override an output, and stop the system safely (Art. 14(4)).
responsible_party: AI provider (design obligation); AI deployer (implementation, via Art. 26(2))
enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Art. 26(2); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37, OJ p. 68 for para. 2; unchanged by 2026/1744); breach finable under Art. 99(4)(e).

exact_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and keep performing consistently throughout their lifecycle. They must be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies (possibly through redundancy or fail-safe plans), manage feedback loops in systems that keep learning, and resist attacks that exploit vulnerabilities. This includes, where appropriate, measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. Accuracy levels and metrics must be declared in the instructions for use.

exact_text: Publish transparency reports that evaluate the risk of harm to individuals and society in the Indian context.
provision_summary: Anyone developing or deploying AI systems in India is advised to publish transparency reports that assess the risk of harm their systems pose to individuals and society in the Indian context. Where a report contains sensitive or proprietary information, it should be shared confidentially with the relevant regulators instead of published.
responsible_party: Developer and deployer ('any person involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India')
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certifications, internal policies, committee hearings, §2.5, PDF p. 33; peer monitoring and third-party audits, §2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).

exact_text: Impose obligations for each of these entities that are proportionate to their function and the risk of harm
provision_summary: The Guidelines recommend clarifying how each actor in the AI value chain (developers, deployers, end-users) is governed under existing law such as the IT Act, and then imposing obligations on each that match its function and the risk of harm (for example transparency reporting, content removal, grievance redressal and legal assistance). This rests on a 'graded liability' model in which responsibility depends on the function performed, the level of risk and whether due diligence was done.
responsible_party: Government (MeitY and sectoral regulators) to clarify and impose obligations; the eventual duty-bearers would be developers, deployers and end-users
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).

exact_text: Develop a risk assessment and classification framework that is customised for India’s local context, and accounts for risks to vulnerable groups.
provision_summary: The Guidelines recommend developing an India-specific framework for assessing and classifying AI risks, based on real-world evidence of harm and reflecting India's social, economic and cultural context, including risks to vulnerable groups such as children and women. Risk mitigation measures would then be applied on the basis of that classification. The Guidelines identify six risk categories: malicious use, bias and discrimination, transparency failures, systemic risks, loss of control, and national security.
responsible_party: Government (developing body not named in the provision; Action Plan says 'with sectoral inputs'; AISI's listed functions include risk analysis)
enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.

exact_text: It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and provide advice to policymakers and industry actors on issues of AI safety.
provision_summary: The AI Safety Institute (AISI) is to be the main body guiding safe and trusted AI in India. It should test and evaluate AI systems for risks and advise policymakers and industry on AI safety. It should also develop draft guidelines, standards, evaluation metrics and testing frameworks with relevant agencies, and promote safety tools for bias mitigation, fairness testing and explainability. The related recommendation asks for adequate resources for AISI to develop testing methods and benchmarks.
responsible_party: AI Safety Institute (IndiaAI Safety Institute), working with agencies and sectoral regulators
enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified. AISI's role is research, testing and advice; the Guidelines give it no powers to compel testing or impose sanctions. It provides risk assessments and 'updates on industry compliance' to TPEC and AIGG (PDF p. 38).

exact_text: The relevant sectoral agencies and regulators should take the lead in monitoring harms, providing guidance and enforcing regulations in their respective domains.
provision_summary: Enforcement is left to existing sectoral agencies and regulators, each within its own domain; for example, the Ministry of Finance and RBI for financial services. MeitY is the nodal ministry for AI adoption and regulation. A new AI Governance Group (AIGG), supported by a Technology & Policy Expert Committee (TPEC), is to coordinate policy across ministries, but it is a coordinating body, not an enforcement authority.
responsible_party: Sectoral regulators and agencies (e.g. RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI, ICMR, NHA, ministries), with MeitY as nodal ministry and AIGG coordinating
enforcement_mechanism: Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. The institutional framework maps regulators to 'Enforcing applicable laws and regulations', 'Supervising compliance' and 'Handling grievances' (PDF pp. 42-43). AIGG is to 'issue guidelines to ensure that firms are held accountable for compliance with local laws' (PDF p. 36).

exact_text: AI systems should be appropriately transparent and explainable.
provision_summary: AI systems should be transparent and explainable to a degree proportionate to their risk. Transparency means communicating appropriate information about an AI system (how, when and for what it is used); explainability means relevant parties can access, interpret and understand its decision-making. Regulators should have enough information to give effect to the other principles. Affected parties should be able to get enough information to enforce their rights. Regulators may ask life cycle actors to provide information in a required form, including through product labelling.
responsible_party: Regulatory authority (implementation through guidance); AI life cycle actors (may be asked by regulators to provide information)
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).

exact_text: Governance measures should be in place to ensure effective oversight of the supply and use of AI systems, with clear lines of accountability established across the AI life cycle.
provision_summary: Organisations across the AI life cycle should have governance measures ensuring effective oversight of how AI systems are supplied and used, with clear lines of accountability. Life cycle actors should take steps to follow the principles, and regulators should place clear compliance expectations on the appropriate actors in the supply chain. Regulators may expect documentation of key decisions, impact assessments or audits where appropriate. The White Paper does not change how legal liability is allocated across the life cycle at this stage.
responsible_party: AI life cycle actors (organisations and individuals that research, design, develop, train, operate, deploy or use AI); regulatory authority (to set expectations)
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).

exact_text: Develop and maintain a cross-economy, society-wide AI risk register to support regulators’ internal risks assessments.
provision_summary: Central government is to run a cross-sectoral risk assessment function. It will develop and maintain an economy-wide AI risk register, monitor and re-prioritise known risks, identify new and emerging risks with the horizon-scanning function, and clarify regulator responsibilities for new or contested risks. It will also identify risks that fall between regulators' remits. The aim is that risks do not fall into gaps and that regulators assess AI risks coherently.
responsible_party: Government (central functions; government will 'initially be responsible for delivering the central functions', para 75, PDF p. 59), working with regulators
enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: an internal government function. Its outputs feed the central monitoring and evaluation function and may lead to advice that further intervention is needed (Box 3.1, PDF p. 49). It includes sharing 'risk enforcement best practices' (PDF p. 51).

exact_text: AI systems should function in a robust, secure and safe way throughout the AI life cycle, and risks should be continually identified, assessed and managed.
provision_summary: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their life cycle, and risks should be continually identified, assessed and managed. Regulators may introduce measures so that systems are technically secure and work reliably as intended. Developers should understand security threats at each life cycle stage and build in resilience, with regulators possibly referring to NCSC machine-learning security principles. Regulators' implementation may require life cycle actors to regularly test or carry out due diligence on a system's functioning, resilience and security, and technical standards may serve as benchmarks.
responsible_party: Regulatory authority (to implement); developer and other AI life cycle actors (testing and due diligence, if required by regulators)
enforcement_mechanism: No new enforcement mechanism. The principles are applied by existing regulators 'using the powers and resources available to them' (para 55, PDF p. 41). Government anticipates, but has not committed to, a statutory duty on regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles (para 57, PDF p. 42), and may not introduce it (para 59). Regulators are encouraged to integrate the principles into existing monitoring, investigation and enforcement processes (para 68, PDF p. 46).

exact_text: Initially, the principles will be issued by government on a non-statutory basis and applied by regulators within their remits.
provision_summary: Existing regulators apply the five principles within their current remits, using their existing powers and resources, during an initial non-statutory period. After that period, and when parliamentary time allows, the government anticipates introducing a statutory duty requiring regulators to 'have due regard' to the principles. It would not introduce the duty if monitoring shows it is unnecessary. There is no new AI regulator.
responsible_party: Regulatory authority (existing sectoral regulators; those named in the White Paper include the ICO, FCA, EHRC and MHRA), supported by central government
enforcement_mechanism: Existing regulators' statutory powers only. Central monitoring and evaluation of the framework (Box 3.1, PDF p. 49). A possible future statutory 'due regard' duty on regulators (para 57), which would bind regulators, not businesses. Regulators must monitor and evaluate their own implementation (para 64, PDF p. 44).

exact_text: AI Actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure regarding AI systems.
provision_summary: AI actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure. They should give meaningful, context-appropriate information so that people understand AI systems' capabilities and limitations, know when they are interacting with AI (including at work), and, where feasible and useful, understand the data, factors and logic behind an output. People adversely affected by an AI system should get information enabling them to challenge its output.
responsible_party: AI actors (Council 'CALLS ON all AI actors', para III); Adherent governments to promote and implement (para II)
enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).

exact_text: AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for the respect of the above principles, based on their roles, the context, and consistent with the state of the art.
provision_summary: AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for respecting the OECD principles, according to their roles and context. To that end they should ensure traceability of datasets, processes and decisions across the lifecycle, so that outputs can be analysed and inquiries answered.
responsible_party: AI actors (those playing an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including those who deploy or operate AI; definitions, p. 8)
enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).

exact_text: AI actors, should, based on their roles, the context, and their ability to act, apply a systematic risk management approach to each phase of the AI system lifecycle on an ongoing basis
provision_summary: AI actors should apply a systematic, ongoing risk management approach to every phase of the AI lifecycle, according to their role, context and ability to act, and adopt responsible business conduct, including by cooperating with suppliers, users and other stakeholders. Risks include harmful bias, human rights (including safety, security and privacy), labour rights and intellectual property rights.
responsible_party: AI actors, with cooperation among AI actors, suppliers of AI knowledge and resources, AI system users and other stakeholders
enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).

exact_text: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their entire lifecycle so that, in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety and/or security risks.
provision_summary: AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their lifecycle, working appropriately and without unreasonable safety or security risks under normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or adverse conditions. There should be mechanisms to override, repair or safely decommission systems that risk undue harm or behave undesirably. Where technically feasible, there should also be mechanisms to bolster information integrity while respecting freedom of expression.
responsible_party: Multiple stakeholders (principle phrased in the passive voice; addressed to AI actors via para III and to Adherents via para II)
enforcement_mechanism: No enforcement or sanctions. Implementation is monitored through the Digital Policy Committee's reports to Council (Section VIII(d), p. 11), practical implementation guidance (VIII(b)) and an information-exchange forum (VIII(c)) (see OECD005).

exact_text: report to Council, in consultation with other relevant committees, on the implementation, dissemination and continued relevance of this Recommendation no later than five years following its revision and at least every ten years thereafter.
provision_summary: The OECD Council instructs its Digital Policy Committee, through the Working Party on AI Governance, to report on how the Recommendation is being implemented, disseminated and kept relevant. Reports are due within five years of the revision and at least every ten years after that. The Committee must also continue its AI work, develop practical implementation guidance and provide a forum for exchanging information.
responsible_party: OECD Digital Policy Committee, through its Working Party on AI Governance (AIGO)
enforcement_mechanism: Periodic reporting to Council and peer exchange only. No sanctions, compliance assessment or dispute mechanism. The 2024 Report to Council found the Recommendation was 'being implemented by its Adherents' (p. 5).
